name: Google Spanner Omni
tagline: Downloadable Spanner that runs on your own servers, other clouds or a laptop, with Paxos and auto-sharding.
description: Spanner Omni is a self-managed edition of Google's Spanner that you can run in your own data center, on AWS or Google Cloud VMs, or on a laptop. Google swapped Spanner's dependencies on Colossus and TrueTime hardware for a local-filesystem storage layer and software time synchronization, while keeping Paxos replication, automatic sharding, and the GoogleSQL, PostgreSQL and graph interfaces, plus vector, full-text and columnar features. It was previewed in April 2026 and reached general availability in autumn 2026 with TLS, authentication, audit logs and backups. There is no availability SLA, and upgrades, monitoring (Prometheus/Grafana) and capacity are your job. A free Developer Edition exists; production use needs a vCPU-based annual subscription.

pricing.notes: Developer Edition free for non-production (single server up to 4 vCPUs does not expire; larger installs get 90-day licenses). Commercial Edition is a vCPU-based annual subscription.

scale.notes: Paxos replication and automatic sharding; Google recommends reference topologies of 3 servers per zone or 3 zones x 3 servers; no SLA.

strengths: Spanner's consistency, auto-sharding and multi-model features outside Google Cloud
Same client libraries and dialects as managed Spanner for portability
Runs on-premises, on AWS, or on a laptop for local development
Free Developer Edition for non-production use
weaknesses: No availability SLA; operations, upgrades and monitoring are on you
Known feature gaps versus managed Spanner, with no public timeline
Google Cloud integrations (BigQuery, Gemini) are unavailable
Very new; little production track record outside Google
useCases: Regulated or sovereign deployments that cannot use public cloud
Hybrid apps sharing a data model with managed Spanner
Multi-cloud distributed SQL with Spanner semantics
Local development and CI against a real Spanner engine
notIdealFor: Small apps that fit one Postgres server
Workloads that require a vendor-backed uptime SLA
